record.title: A controlled agent-population study finds indirect convention shifts can lower tipping thresholds
record.summary: A September 21 preprint studies how committed minorities can redirect conventions in homogeneous, fully connected naming-game populations of four open-weight LLMs. The authors report that fewer than 10% of single-intermediate paths reduce total committed effort versus a direct transition. In evaluated triplets, allowing a third convention during a single stage produces cost-effective transitions in 15–40% of cases across model populations, compared with 12–23% for isolated two-stage routes. These are results from a controlled model, not observed attacks or evidence about deployed heterogeneous agent networks.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The preprint defines and evaluates a repeated naming-game model with homogeneous, fully connected populations instantiated from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Phi-4, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that fewer than 10% of single-intermediate paths reduce additive committed effort below the direct-transition requirement; this fraction declines for longer paths.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across evaluated model populations, an integrated single-stage approach with a third convention available yields cost-effective transitions in 15–40% of cases, versus 12–23% for isolated two-stage routes over the same triplets.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The results concern a controlled naming-game model with homogeneous populations; the paper does not demonstrate attacks on deployed heterogeneous agent networks or validate real-world intervention success.

evidence_gaps.description: The reported model outcomes were not independently reproduced in this activation.
No evidence in the paper establishes that these convention dynamics occur in heterogeneous, deployed agent populations.

brief.importance_rationale: If analogous tipping pathways occur in deployed interacting-agent populations, attackers or accidental perturbations could redirect collective conventions through intermediate states, changing how stability is assessed. Score 6 reflects the potential consequence of this bounded mechanism; the evidence is a controlled naming-game study, not a field demonstration.
limitations: This is a preprint and the findings are author-reported; no independent reproduction was run here.
The model uses homogeneous, fully connected populations and a naming-game coordination task, which narrows transfer to real agent networks.
The authors state that fewer than 10% of single-intermediate routes are sub-additive; advantageous routes are the exception in the modeled landscape.
No deployed attack, field measurement or validated defense is shown.
brief.summary: A September 21 preprint studies how committed minorities can redirect conventions in homogeneous, fully connected naming-game populations of four open-weight LLMs. The authors report that fewer than 10% of single-intermediate paths reduce total committed effort versus a direct transition. In evaluated triplets, allowing a third convention during a single stage produces cost-effective transitions in 15–40% of cases across model populations, compared with 12–23% for isolated two-stage routes. These are results from a controlled model, not observed attacks or evidence about deployed heterogeneous agent networks.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report fewer than 10% of single-intermediate paths are sub-additive. For evaluated triplets, integrated single-stage competition with an additional available convention gives cost-effective transitions in 15–40% of cases versus 12–23% for isolated two-stage routes across the four modeled populations.
technical.compute_or_cost: Not a hardware or inference-cost result; transition cost is measured as committed population fraction and related path objectives.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint presents a model and reports simulated results over four homogeneous LLM populations; this activation inspected the paper text but did not rerun the simulations.
technical.implementation_status: Research model in a preprint; no deployed system or operational attack demonstrated.
technical.mechanism: Pairwise convention transitions are assigned critical-mass thresholds and connected into a directed transition landscape; path optimization then compares direct and intermediate routes, with both additive and maximum commitment costs.
technical.regime: Homogeneous, fully connected naming-game populations using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Phi-4, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B; controlled convention sets and committed minority interventions.
technical.reproducibility: Methods and supplementary figures are described in the preprint; no independent reproduction or model execution was performed in this activation.
technical.strongest_baseline: Direct pairwise convention transition; the comparison also includes isolated multi-stage paths over the same evaluated triplets.

brief.title: A controlled agent-population study finds indirect convention shifts can lower tipping thresholds
brief.why_it_matters: The paper suggests that pairwise tests of an agent population’s resistance may miss paths through intermediate conventions, while also finding those cost-reducing paths are uncommon in its model. If such structure transfers to deployed systems, safety evaluations may need to consider the available convention set and sequences of interventions. No real-world attack or mitigation effectiveness is established.
